chunks: Implementing power sequencing. The question: How can you implement power sequencing?
Once you know the order rails must start in, you need hardware to enforce it. The simplest method is to let one regulator's "I am ready" signal switch on the next regulator.
If you need a pause between steps, you add a small resistor-capacitor delay. Bigger systems use a dedicated sequencer chip or a small controller.
Think of a relay race. The second runner may not start until the baton arrives, so no one has to guess a time.
Adding a delay is like making the second runner count to five after receiving the baton.
A weakness of the race: if the baton passes late or early, the whole chain shifts, and an RC delay can vary a lot with part tolerances.
PG-to-EN chaining with an optional RC delay. Reg A's open-drain PG is pulled up to 3. 3 volts through R pu .
When Reg A's output is valid, PG releases and C d charges through R pu plus R d , and Reg B turns on when the EN node crosses its threshold.
Reg A's EN is tied to V in (or a UVLO divider) so it starts first.
Enable (EN) pin: an input that turns a regulator on when its voltage rises above a threshold, often about 1 volts.
Power-good (PG): an output that says the regulator's output is valid ("Power sequencing: why, order, timing").
Open-drain: an output that can only pull low, so it needs a pull-up resistor to go high ("Pull-up and pull-down resistors").
RC delay: a resistor feeding a capacitor, so the capacitor's voltage rises slowly instead of jumping.
Supervisor: a chip that watches a voltage and releases a signal after a set delay.
Rail A comes from regulator A. Its PG pin has a pull-up resistor to 3. 3 volts and also connects to the EN pin of regulator B. While A is not valid, PG pulls low and B stays off.
When A is valid, PG is released and the pull-up lifts EN above its threshold, so B starts.
To add delay, make the total resistance feeding EN 100 kilohms and put 100 nanofarads from EN to ground. The time constant is RC equals 10 milliseconds, and EN crosses a 1.
2 volts threshold after about 4. 5 milliseconds. That is the whole idea.
"The simplest is to chain regulators: the power-good pin of one, pulled up through a resistor, drives the enable of the next, so each rail starts only when the previous is valid.
For extra delay I add an RC on the enable, with t equals RC log [V cc over (V cc-V th)] , though tolerance is loose.
For more control I use a voltage supervisor, or a sequencer IC or PMIC, or an MCU or CPLD reading PGs. Tracking pins and load switches handle ramps and gating.
I reverse the same logic for power-down and verify on a scope across temperature."
